Two pneumatic presses can look identical and behave nothing alike. Open (tank) presses are simpler and cheaper and let you process quickly; closed presses run under inert gas or reduced oxygen for whites and delicate styles where oxidation is the enemy. Then there's drainage design, axial channels versus a plain perforated basket, which decides how fast and how cleanly the juice comes off. Membrane material and cycle programming set how gently you can press. Read past the hectolitre rating to how the press actually works, then browse by configuration and capacity.

Crossflow and plate-and-frame filtration reach the same clarity by very different routes. Crossflow runs wine tangentially across a membrane, self-cleaning as it goes: one machine, minimal consumables, tight and repeatable filtration, at a higher upfront cost. Plate-and-frame uses pads or sheets, a lower entry price, but labor to load and change, filter media to buy, and more hands-on operation each run. Small-lot cellars often start with pads; volume operations move to crossflow to kill the labor and consumable cost. Which one pays back depends on how much wine you push. Compare them on your throughput.

Sizing fermentation tanks is less about total volume than about lot size. Ten thousand litres in one tank and the same in four tanks are different wineries — the four-tank setup ferments small lots separately, blends on purpose, and isolates a problem before it spreads. But every tank you add costs capital and floor space, and an oversized tank run half-full invites oxidation unless it's variable-capacity. The honest sizing question is: how many distinct lots will you actually make, now and in five years? Answer that, then size. The calculator walks through the math.

On a fermentation tank, the weld is where quality hides. A poorly-made seam corrodes, harbors spoilage organisms in its crevices, and quietly undoes your sanitation program vintage after vintage. What you want: continuous, ground-and-polished internal welds, low-carbon 316L at the contact surfaces to resist carbide precipitation, and documented weld procedures you can actually ask for. Traceable welds aren't a luxury spec — they're the difference between a tank you clean and a tank you fight. We vet suppliers on exactly this before they reach your shortlist. Craft meets commerce.

Stainless, oak, or concrete — the fermentation vessel shapes the wine as much as the fruit does. Stainless is inert, precise, and easy to clean: it holds temperature, protects fruit-forward aromatics, and gives you total control. Oak breathes, softens tannin, and adds texture and spice, at the cost of upkeep and neutrality over time. Concrete sits between — some micro-oxygenation without oak flavor. Most cellars end up with a mix matched to the wines they make, not a single dogma. Decide what each wine needs before you buy the vessel, not after. The guide lays out the trade-offs.

Most oxidation problems aren't the wine — they're the transfer. Every rack, every pump-over, every move between tanks is a chance to pick up oxygen and shear delicate structure. The pump you choose decides how much. A flexible-impeller or progressive-cavity pump run gently moves wine at low shear; a centrifugal pump run hard whips air into it. Match the pump to the wine's fragility and the flow to the job — slow for finished reds, careful for aromatic whites. The transfer stage is invisible until it shows up in the glass as flatness. Spec it deliberately.

Low-shear transfer is one of those specs that sounds like jargon until you taste what happens without it. Shear is the mechanical stress a pump puts on wine — high shear tears at lees, strips texture, and pulls in oxygen. For moving wine on its lees, or racking a barrel-aged red you've spent a year building, a gentle positive-displacement pump protects everything you've made. The wrong pump can undo months of careful work in one careless transfer. Ask about the pump type and the achievable flow range, not just the connection size. Gentle is a spec, not a promise.

Tri-clamp or DIN? It's a small fitting that shapes your whole cellar. Tri-clamp connections are quick to assemble, easy to inspect, and the North American sanitary default — pop the clamp, check the gasket, reassemble in seconds. DIN fittings are the European standard, threaded and robust, common on equipment sourced from Italian and French makers. Neither is wrong; mixing them without adapters is the headache. Before you buy a pump or a length of hose, know which standard your tanks, valves, and press already speak. Consistency here saves you a drawer full of adapters and a lot of swearing during crush.

Crossflow or plate-and-frame? The trade is automation and consistency against upfront cost. A crossflow (tangential-flow) system runs the wine parallel to the membrane so solids don't cake it — one closed, automated pass, less oxygen pickup, no pads to buy or dispose of. Plate-and-frame costs far less to acquire but is labor-heavy, exposes wine to more air, and turns pads into a running cost and a waste stream. For steady volume, crossflow often wins on total cost despite the sticker; for occasional small lots, plate-and-frame still earns its place. Run your volumes before you decide.

The most common sizing mistake on a fermentation tank is buying to your grape weight and forgetting the cap. Red ferments need headspace: ullage for the rising cap, room for punch-downs or pump-overs, space so you're not cleaning must off the ceiling. A tank filled to the brim on paper is overfilled in practice. As a rule of thumb, size the vessel above your must volume, not level with it, and match jacket coverage to your peak fermentation heat. The sizing guide walks through the math with real numbers so you don't learn this during crush.
